metadata.title: Important-Things-to-Know-Before-Developing-Artific
metadata.venue: International Journal of Online Pedagogy and Course Design

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study used a small, school-based drone learning intervention in Taiwan (two elementary and two junior high schools) with a pre/post attainment test and post-task questionnaires/checklists. The manuscript does not report any complex survey design, sampling weights, or replicate-weight procedures (e.g., BRR/jackknife), and it does not name any weight variables. Because the analysis is based on a recruited convenience sample across four schools rather than an ILSA-style nationally representative design, population-representative weighting is not described. For replication, analysts should treat the results as unweighted within-sample estimates unless the authors provide a weighting scheme; no PV/scaling weights apply because the outcomes are researcher-developed tests and self-report scales rather than ILSA PV achievement scores.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables are (a) researcher-developed multiple-choice attainment test scores and (b) questionnaire/checklist scale means (motivated strategies and computational thinking), not PV-based cognitive achievement scores from an ILSA assessment. As a result, plausible values are not generated or combined across PV draws. The manuscript also does not describe any missing-data handling procedure (e.g., exclusion rules or imputation), which is a reporting gap for transparency, especially given the multi-instrument design (pre/post test plus multiple self-report factors).

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analytic sample comprised 73 learners recruited from four schools (A–D) in Taoyuan City, Taiwan, aged 11–15, who completed the drone learning module and participated in the pre- and post-attainment testing and post-task questionnaires/checklists. The manuscript describes the intervention as three days of summer camp with task-based drone activities and reports pre/post means for the same group, implying paired participation. No additional inclusion/exclusion criteria (e.g., missing-item rules, grade-only restrictions, or attrition handling) are explicitly stated; therefore, the study appears to use the available participants who completed the full learning sequence and assessments.

main_findings.dataset_used: Drone learning module (Taiwan Taoyuan) — pre/post attainment test (Blockly for Robolink), ages 11–15
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multiple regression: R2 = 0.20 (adjusted R2 = 0.17). Predictors: Problem-solving β = 0.313, t = 2.746, p < .01; Creativity β = -0.276, t = -2.304, p < .05; Gender β = 0.217, t = 1.909 (not significant). Pre/post mean change: M = 22.89 (SD = 9.75) to M = 48.63 (SD = 16.92), paired t-test t = 24.051***.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using the drone learning module data (Taiwan Taoyuan) with Blockly-for-Robolink attainment test scores, the study leveraged Gender, Problem-solving, and Creativity to predict programming attainment, finding that Problem-solving was a significant positive predictor while Creativity was a significant negative predictor (R2 = 0.20). This indicates that strengthening learners’ problem-solving processes in collaborative drone programming may improve programming attainment, while creativity measures may relate differently to attainment in this task design (and causality cannot be inferred from this correlational regression).

main_findings.dataset_used: Drone learning module (Taiwan Taoyuan) — motivated strategies questionnaire after learning
main_findings.target_variable: Motivated strategies dimensions (self-efficacy vs metacognition/effort regulation/critical thinking)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Repeat-measures ANOVA: Greenhouse-Geisser ε = 0.81, F[2.42, 70.58] = 27.97, p < 0.001. Means (M, SD): Metacognition 4.18 (0.33), Effort regulation 4.28 (0.32), Critical thinking 4.06 (0.39), Self-efficacy 3.88 (0.54). Post hoc: Self-efficacy significantly lower than other dimensions.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using the drone learning module questionnaire the study leveraged self-efficacy, metacognition, effort regulation, and critical thinking dimensions to characterize motivated strategies after learning, finding that self-efficacy was significantly lower than metacognition, effort regulation, and critical thinking (ANOVA F = 27.97, p < .001). This indicates that drone STEAM interventions may build self-regulatory and thinking skills without automatically increasing learners’ confidence, so educators should add targeted supports to improve self-efficacy alongside metacognitive scaffolding.

main_findings.dataset_used: Drone learning module (Taiwan Taoyuan) — computational thinking checklist after learning
main_findings.target_variable: Computational thinking dimensions (cooperativity vs algorithmic thinking/creativity/problem-solving)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Repeat-measures ANOVA: Greenhouse-Geisser ε = 0.76, F[2.29, 70.71] = 50.09, p < 0.001. Means (M, SD): Creativity 3.99 (0.37), Algorithmic thinking 3.62 (0.36), Problem-solving 3.37 (0.48), Cooperativity 4.3 (0.38). Post hoc: Cooperativity significantly higher than algorithmic thinking, creativity, and problem-solving. Correlation: Problem-solving and algorithmic thinking r = .542**.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using the drone learning module computational thinking checklist the study leveraged cooperativity, algorithmic thinking, creativity, and problem-solving to characterize computational thinking after learning, finding that cooperativity was the highest-rated dimension and that problem-solving and algorithmic thinking were moderately correlated (r = .542, p < .01). This indicates that collaborative structures in drone programming may be especially effective for fostering cooperative computational thinking, suggesting that group-based scaffolding should be a core design element in distributed expertise learning systems.

data.outcome_summary: This study reports a small, school-based drone learning intervention in Taiwan (Taoyuan City) with 73 learners aged 11–15 who completed task-based drone activities using Blockly for Robolink. The main quantitative outcomes were (1) a researcher-developed pre/post attainment test of drone concepts and Blockly programming and (2) post-task questionnaires/checklists measuring motivated strategies (metacognition, effort regulation, critical thinking, self-efficacy) and computational thinking (creativity, algorithmic thinking, problem-solving, cooperativity). Programming attainment increased from M = 22.89 (SD = 9.75) to M = 48.63 (SD = 16.92), and multiple regression showed Problem-solving (β = .313, p < .01) and Creativity (β = −.276, p < .05) as significant predictors (R2 = 0.20). Motivated strategies differed by dimension, with self-efficacy significantly lower than other self-regulatory factors (ANOVA F = 27.97, p < .001). The computational thinking checklist similarly showed cooperativity as the highest dimension (ANOVA F = 50.09, p < .001). Limitations include the absence of ML model training/metrics, no reported missing-data handling, and no survey-weighting or PV framework because outcomes are not ILSA PV-based achievement scores.
